label: Issue 1
what: The Arkansas Constitution already requires voters to be U.S. citizens. Issue 1 (HJR 1018) rewrites Article 3 to say that only U.S. citizens meeting the existing qualifications may vote, and that anyone who doesn't meet them may not vote in any state or local election. The four existing qualifications stay the same.
y: The Constitution is reworded to say only U.S. citizens may vote in state and local elections.
n: The current wording, which already requires citizenship, stays.
fiscal: No fiscal estimate published; the U of A Public Policy Center notes it makes no change to the existing qualifications. Takes effect Jan 1, 2027.
pro: Rep. David Ray, Sen. John Payton (sponsors), Americans for Citizen Voting

label: Issue 2
t: Expand constitutional right to keep and bear arms
what: Amends Article 2, Section 5 (SJR 11) to say the right to keep and bear arms covers common defense, lawful hunting, recreation and any other lawful purpose. It specifies that the right includes possessing and using ammunition, firearm accessories and components, and calls it a natural, fundamental, individual right that shall not be infringed.
y: The state constitution spells out a broader right to bear arms, including ammunition and accessories.
n: The existing Article 2, Section 5 wording stays.
pro: Sen. John Payton, Rep. Matt Duffield (sponsors)

label: Issue 3
what: Lets the Legislature create programs, loans and grants using public money for economic development (SJR 15), and pass laws letting cities, counties or cooperative areas set up economic development districts. Property in a district would be exempt from regular property taxes and could instead be taxed and charged fees by the district, which could issue bonds repaid from any district funds. The amendment creates no district itself; details would come in later legislation.
y: The Legislature may create economic development grants, loans and taxing districts.
n: Current constitutional limits on these programs and districts stay.
fiscal: No official dollar estimate; effects depend on implementing legislation and any districts local governments create.
pro: Sen. Jonathan Dismang, Rep. Howard Beaty (sponsors); supporters cite competing with neighboring states
con: Opponents (per U of A Public Policy Center) argue it shifts property-tax burden off district property and amounts to corporate subsidies

label: Issue 4
what: Authorizes the Arkansas Natural Resources Commission to issue up to $500M in general obligation bonds (Act 578 of 2025) for water, waste disposal, pollution control, drainage, irrigation, flood control and wetlands projects. No more than $165M may go to irrigation, and no more than $60M can be issued in any two-year period without legislative approval. Bonds are backed by the state's full faith and credit.
y: The state can borrow up to $500M for water and wastewater projects and loans.
n: No new bonds; lawmakers would need general revenue or other sources to match federal water funds.
fiscal: Up to $500M principal repaid over at most 35 years; debt service has first claim on state general revenue and is partly repaid from local loan repayments. The 2008 $300M authorization is nearly spent. Takes effect July 1, 2027.
pro: Sen. Bart Hester, Rep. Howard Beaty Jr. (sponsors), Arkansas Natural Resources Commission
con: Critics (per U of A Public Policy Center) cite interest costs and broad eligibility

reasons.fiscal: Adds up to $500M in state general obligation debt repaid from general revenue over up to 35 years.
reasons.services: Funds grants and loans for local drinking-water, sewer and flood-control systems and federal revolving-fund matches.
